sections.title: What is a Dataclass? — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is a dataclass and what boilerplate code does it automatically generate?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> A dataclass is a Python decorator (`@dataclass`) introduced in Python 3.7 (PEP 557) that automatically generates boilerplate special methods for classes whose primary purpose is storing data. By default it generates: `__init__()` (constructor with all fields as parameters), `__repr__()` (human-readable string representation), and `__eq__()` (equality comparison that compares all fields). Optionally with parameters: `order=True` generates `__lt__`, `__le__`, `__gt__`, `__ge__`; `frozen=True` generates `__hash__` and makes instances immutable. Before dataclasses, writing a proper data class required 30+ lines for what's now 4 lines. I use dataclasses for all data-holding classes: API models, database row representations, configuration objects, event messages.

**Q2. What is the difference between a dataclass and a regular Python class?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> A regular Python class requires you to manually write `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__` and other dunder methods. A dataclass auto-generates them from field annotations. Key differences: (1) Dataclasses require **type annotations** for all fields — they're not just code style, they're part of the dataclass specification. (2) `__eq__` in regular classes defaults to identity comparison (`is`); dataclass `__eq__` compares ALL field values. (3) `__repr__` in regular classes shows just the class name and memory address; dataclass `__repr__` shows all field names and values. (4) Dataclasses have `field()`, `asdict()`, `astuple()`, `fields()`, `replace()` utilities. Use dataclass when: primary purpose is holding structured data. Use regular class when: complex behavior, heavy method logic, inheritance with complex MRO.

**Q3. Why must fields with default values come AFTER fields without defaults in a dataclass?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> This is the same constraint as Python function parameters — you can't have a required parameter after an optional one. Since `@dataclass` generates `__init__` where fields with defaults become keyword arguments with defaults and fields without defaults become required positional arguments, Python's function signature rules apply. `def __init__(self, name: str, age: int = 0)` is valid but `def __init__(self, age: int = 0, name: str)` is a `SyntaxError`. So `@dataclass class Person: name: str; age: int = 0` works, but `age: int = 0; name: str` raises `TypeError`. The fix for mutable defaults (lists, dicts) is using `field(default_factory=list)` — never use `names: list = []` as it shares one list across all instances (classic mutable default argument bug).

**Q4. What is `__post_init__()` and when do you use it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `__post_init__()` is a special method automatically called by the dataclass-generated `__init__()` AFTER all field assignments are complete. Use it for: (1) **Validation** — check field values and raise errors: `if self.age < 0: raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative")`. (2) **Computed fields** — derive field values from others: `self.full_name = f"{self.first_name} {self.last_name}"`. (3) **Type conversion** — convert types: `self.tags = list(self.tags) if isinstance(self.tags, tuple) else self.tags`. (4) **Setting fields that depend on other fields**. I use `__post_init__` extensively for business rule validation in domain models. It's cleaner than overriding `__init__` because you still get all the dataclass magic.

**Q5. Can a dataclass have methods? Can it inherit from other classes?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Yes to both! Dataclasses are still regular Python classes — the decorator just adds auto-generated methods. You can add: regular methods, class methods, static methods, properties, and any special methods. Properties are very useful in dataclasses — they appear in code but NOT in `__repr__` or `__eq__` (only actual fields do). For inheritance: dataclasses can inherit from regular classes and other dataclasses. Child dataclass fields come AFTER parent fields in `__init__`. Important rule: if parent has fields with defaults, child cannot have fields without defaults (breaks `__init__` signature). For abstract base classes: use `@dataclass` with `ABC`. I use dataclass inheritance for building hierarchies like: `BaseEntity` → `Product`, `User`, `Order` — where `BaseEntity` has `id`, `created_at`, `updated_at`.

sections.title: What is a Dataclass? — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**S1. Your team stores API response data in plain dictionaries. How would you improve this using dataclasses?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict
> from typing import List, Optional
> from datetime import datetime
>
> # ❌ BEFORE: plain dict — no type safety, no IDE autocomplete,
> # no validation, typos cause runtime errors
> def process_user_dict(user_data: dict):
>     # What keys exist? Have to check docs or guess
>     name  = user_data["naem"]    # TYPO! KeyError at runtime!
>     email = user_data.get("email", "")
>     # No autocomplete, no type checking
>
> # ✅ AFTER: dataclass — type-safe, self-documenting, IDE support
> @dataclass
> class UserProfile:
>     user_id:    int
>     username:   str
>     email:      str
>     full_name:  str
>     is_active:  bool         = True
>     role:       str          = "user"
>     tags:       List[str]    = field(default_factory=list)
>     last_login: Optional[str]= None
>     created_at: str          = field(default_factory=lambda: datetime.now().isoformat())
>
>     def __post_init__(self):
>         # Validation
>         if not self.email or "@" not in self.email:
>             raise ValueError(f"Invalid email: {self.email}")
>         if not self.username:
>             raise ValueError("Username cannot be empty")
>         # Normalization
>         self.email    = self.email.lower().strip()
>         self.username = self.username.strip()
>
>     @property
>     def display_name(self) -> str:
>         return self.full_name or self.username
>
>     @classmethod
>     def from_api_response(cls, data: dict) -> "UserProfile":
>         """Factory method to create from API response dict"""
>         return cls(
>             user_id   = data["id"],
>             username  = data["username"],
>             email     = data["email"],
>             full_name = data.get("full_name", ""),
>             is_active = data.get("is_active", True),
>             role      = data.get("role", "user"),
>             tags      = data.get("tags", []),
>             last_login= data.get("last_login"),
>         )
>
>     def to_dict(self) -> dict:
>         """Convert to dict for JSON serialization"""
>         return asdict(self)
>
> # API response simulation
> api_response = {
>     "id": 1001, "username": "alice_j",
>     "email": "Alice@Example.COM",
>     "full_name": "Alice Johnson",
>     "role": "admin", "tags": ["python", "developer"],
>     "last_login": "2024-01-15T10:30:00"
> }
>
> user = UserProfile.from_api_response(api_response)
> print(f"User    : {user.display_name}")   # IDE autocomplete works!
> print(f"Email   : {user.email}")          # auto-lowercased
> print(f"Tags    : {user.tags}")
> print(f"Dict    : {user.to_dict()}")
>
> # Type safety in action
> try:
>     invalid = UserProfile(1, "bob", "not-an-email", "Bob")
> except ValueError as e:
>     print(f"Validation caught: {e}")
> ```

**S2. You're building a configuration system. Why use a frozen dataclass instead of a regular dict?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace
> from typing import Tuple
>
> # ❌ PROBLEM with dict config: mutable, no type safety,
> # can accidentally modify, no validation
> config_dict = {"host": "localhost", "port": 8080}
> config_dict["port"] = "wrong_type"  # No error! Silent bug
>
> # ✅ SOLUTION: frozen dataclass — immutable, typed, hashable
> @dataclass(frozen=True)  # frozen = immutable after creation
> class DatabaseConfig:
>     host:         str
>     port:         int
>     database:     str
>     user:         str
>     password:     str
>     pool_size:    int   = 5
>     timeout:      int   = 30
>     ssl:          bool  = False
>     allowed_hosts:Tuple[str, ...] = ("localhost",)
>
>     def __post_init__(self):
>         if not 1 <= self.port <= 65535:
>             raise ValueError(f"Invalid port: {self.port}")
>         if self.pool_size < 1:
>             raise ValueError("pool_size must be >= 1")
>
>     @property
>     def connection_string(self) -> str:
>         return (f"postgresql://{self.user}:***@"
>                 f"{self.host}:{self.port}/{self.database}")
>
> @dataclass(frozen=True)
> class AppConfig:
>     database:    DatabaseConfig
>     debug:       bool  = False
>     log_level:   str   = "INFO"
>     api_version: str   = "v1"
>
> # Create config
> db_cfg = DatabaseConfig(
>     host="prod-db.example.com",
>     port=5432,
>     database="myapp",
>     user="app_user",
>     password="secret",
>     pool_size=10,
>     ssl=True,
>     allowed_hosts=("prod-db.example.com", "replica.example.com")
> )
>
> app_cfg = AppConfig(database=db_cfg, log_level="WARNING")
>
> # Frozen = cannot modify!
> try:
>     app_cfg.debug = True  # AttributeError!
> except Exception as e:
>     print(f"Cannot modify frozen: {e}")
>
> # Instead: create modified COPY using replace()
> debug_cfg = replace(app_cfg, debug=True, log_level="DEBUG")
> print(f"Original debug: {app_cfg.debug}")   # False — unchanged
> print(f"New debug     : {debug_cfg.debug}") # True
>
> # Hashable! Can use as dict key or in sets
> config_cache = {app_cfg: "cached_result_1"}
> print(f"Used as dict key: {config_cache[app_cfg]}")
>
> print(f"\nDB Connection: {db_cfg.connection_string}")
> print(f"Log Level    : {app_cfg.log_level}")
> ```

**S3. You need to compare, sort, and deduplicate a collection of Product objects. How do dataclasses help?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field, astuple
> from typing import List
>
> @dataclass(order=True)  # enables <, >, <=, >=
> class Product:
>     # Fields used for ordering are first (order compares field by field)
>     price:       float
>     name:        str
>     # Non-ordering fields
>     category:    str  = field(compare=False)  # exclude from eq AND order
>     in_stock:    bool = field(compare=False)
>     description: str  = field(default="", compare=False, repr=False)
>
> # Create products
> products = [
>     Product(999.99, "Laptop Pro",     "Electronics", True),
>     Product(29.99,  "Mouse",          "Accessories", True),
>     Product(449.99, "Monitor 27in",   "Electronics", False),
>     Product(29.99,  "Keyboard",       "Accessories", True),  # same price as Mouse
>     Product(999.99, "Laptop Pro",     "Electronics", True),  # duplicate!
>     Product(79.99,  "USB Hub",        "Accessories", True),
> ]
>
> print("=== Sorting (by price, then name) ===")
> sorted_products = sorted(products)
> for p in sorted_products:
>     print(f"  ${p.price:>8.2f}  {p.name}")
>
> print("\n=== Most expensive 3 ===")
> top3 = sorted(products, reverse=True)[:3]
> for p in top3:
>     print(f"  ${p.price:.2f}  {p.name}")
>
> print("\n=== Deduplication ===")
> # __eq__ compares price + name (compare=False fields excluded)
> seen     = []
> unique   = []
> for p in products:
>     if p not in seen:
>         seen.append(p)
>         unique.append(p)
> print(f"Original: {len(products)}, After dedup: {len(unique)}")
>
> print("\n=== Price comparison ===")
> laptop = Product(999.99, "Laptop Pro", "Electronics", True)
> mouse  = Product(29.99, "Mouse",      "Accessories", True)
> print(f"Laptop > Mouse  : {laptop > mouse}")   # True (999.99 > 29.99)
> print(f"Laptop == Laptop: {laptop == Product(999.99,'Laptop Pro','Other',False)}")
> # True! category and in_stock have compare=False
>
> print("\n=== In-stock expensive products ===")
> expensive_in_stock = [p for p in products
>                       if p.price > 100 and p.in_stock]
> for p in expensive_in_stock:
>     print(f"  {p.name}: ${p.price:.2f}")
> ```

sections.title: Field Definitions & the field() Function — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. Why can't you use a mutable default value like `[]` directly in a dataclass field? How do you fix it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> This is the classic Python mutable default argument bug. If you write `items: list = []`, Python creates ONE list object at class definition time, shared across ALL instances. Adding to one instance's list modifies ALL instances. `@dataclass` actually protects you here — it raises `ValueError: mutable default <class 'list'> for field items is not allowed: use default_factory`. The fix is `field(default_factory=list)` — this calls `list()` fresh for EACH new instance. For dict: `field(default_factory=dict)`. For custom objects: `field(default_factory=lambda: MyObject())`. This is such a common Python gotcha that I make it a mandatory code review item for any class definition.

**Q2. What is the difference between `compare=False` and `repr=False` in `field()`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `compare=False` excludes a field from BOTH `__eq__` and ordering comparisons (`__lt__`, etc.). Use this for: internal state tracking (`login_count`, `cache`), computed values that mirror other fields, audit fields like `updated_at` that shouldn't affect logical equality. `repr=False` excludes a field from `__repr__` display. Use this for: sensitive data (`password_hash`, `api_key`, `token`), large data that clutters output (`content`, `raw_data`), internal/private fields. They're independent — a field can be `compare=True, repr=False` (compared but not shown) or `compare=False, repr=True` (shown but not compared). I use both regularly: `repr=False` for all sensitive fields, `compare=False` for audit timestamps.

**Q3. What does `init=False` do and when do you use it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `init=False` means the field is NOT included in the generated `__init__` — it cannot be passed as a constructor argument. The value is set either in `__post_init__` or using the `default`/`default_factory`. Common uses: (1) Auto-generated IDs: `id: str = field(default_factory=lambda: str(uuid4()), init=False)`. (2) Computed fields from other fields: `full_name: str = field(default="", init=False)` — set in `__post_init__`. (3) Timestamps: `created_at: str = field(default_factory=..., init=False)`. (4) Internal state: `_cache: dict = field(default_factory=dict, init=False, repr=False)`. Key insight: if you need a field that's ALWAYS computed (never passed by caller), use `init=False`. If caller might sometimes pass it, keep it in `__init__` with a default.

**Q4. What is `kw_only=True` in a field and why is it useful?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `kw_only=True` (Python 3.10+) forces that specific field to be passed as a keyword argument only — it cannot be passed positionally. This prevents argument order confusion when you have multiple fields of the same type. Example: without `kw_only`, `Person("Alice", "Smith", "Chicago")` — which arg is last name vs city? With `kw_only=True` on city: `Person("Alice", "Smith", city="Chicago")` — explicit and clear. I use `kw_only=True` for: any field where positional passing would be ambiguous, optional fields that come after required ones, payment-related fields where order mistakes have consequences (`amount`, `currency`). You can also use `@dataclass(kw_only=True)` to make ALL fields keyword-only.

**Q5. What is `field(metadata=...)` used for?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `metadata` is a read-only mapping (dict-like) attached to a field for use by external code — the dataclass itself ignores it completely. It's a way to attach arbitrary information to fields for consumption by libraries, ORMs, validators, form generators, serializers, or any other code that inspects dataclass fields via `fields()`. Common uses: (1) ORM column definitions: `metadata={"db_column": "email_address", "max_length": 255}`. (2) Form generation: `metadata={"label": "Email", "widget": "email_input"}`. (3) API documentation: `metadata={"description": "User email", "example": "user@example.com"}`. (4) Validation rules: `metadata={"min": 0, "max": 100}`. Access via `dataclasses.fields(MyClass)[0].metadata`. Libraries like `marshmallow`, SQLAlchemy, and FastAPI leverage this pattern.

**S2. Your dataclass has a password field that should never appear in logs or debug output but still be compared for equality tests. How do you configure this?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field
> import hashlib
>
> @dataclass
> class Credentials:
>     username:      str
>     # repr=False: never shown in print/repr/logs
>     # compare=True (default): included in equality checks
>     password_hash: str = field(repr=False)
>     api_key:       str = field(repr=False, compare=False)  # hidden AND not compared
>
>     @classmethod
>     def create(cls, username: str, password: str, api_key: str = "") -> "Credentials":
>         """Hash password before storing"""
>         hashed = hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()
>         return cls(username=username, password_hash=hashed, api_key=api_key)
>
>     def verify_password(self, password: str) -> bool:
>         return self.password_hash == hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()
>
> creds = Credentials.create("alice", "secret123", "api-key-xyz")
> print(f"Creds: {creds}")
> # Credentials(username='alice')  ← password_hash and api_key NOT shown!
>
> # But equality DOES compare password_hash (compare=True by default)
> creds2 = Credentials.create("alice", "secret123", "different-key")
> print(f"Equal (same pass): {creds == creds2}")  # True (api_key excluded)
>
> creds3 = Credentials.create("alice", "wrong_pass", "api-key-xyz")
> print(f"Equal (diff pass): {creds == creds3}")  # False!
>
> print(f"Valid password: {creds.verify_password('secret123')}")  # True
> print(f"Wrong password: {creds.verify_password('wrongpass')}")  # False
> ```

**S3. You need a dataclass where some fields are auto-computed from other fields, not passed by the user. Design it.**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field
> from typing import List
> import hashlib, uuid
> from datetime import datetime
>
> @dataclass
> class PurchaseOrder:
>     # User provides these
>     vendor_name:  str
>     items:        List[dict]   # [{"name":"Widget","qty":5,"price":2.99}]
>     tax_rate:     float = 0.08
>
>     # AUTO-GENERATED — not in __init__ (init=False)
>     order_id:     str   = field(default="", init=False)
>     created_at:   str   = field(default="", init=False)
>     subtotal:     float = field(default=0.0, init=False)
>     tax_amount:   float = field(default=0.0, init=False)
>     total:        float = field(default=0.0, init=False)
>     item_count:   int   = field(default=0,   init=False)
>     checksum:     str   = field(default="", init=False, repr=False)
>
>     def __post_init__(self):
>         # All computed fields set here
>         self.order_id   = f"PO-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8].upper()}"
>         self.created_at = datetime.now().isoformat()
>         self.subtotal   = sum(i["qty"] * i["price"] for i in self.items)
>         self.tax_amount = round(self.subtotal * self.tax_rate, 2)
>         self.total      = round(self.subtotal + self.tax_amount, 2)
>         self.item_count = sum(i["qty"] for i in self.items)
>         # Integrity checksum
>         data = f"{self.order_id}{self.total}{self.vendor_name}"
>         self.checksum = hashlib.md5(data.encode()).hexdigest()
>
>     def verify_integrity(self) -> bool:
>         data = f"{self.order_id}{self.total}{self.vendor_name}"
>         return self.checksum == hashlib.md5(data.encode()).hexdigest()
>
> # User only provides business data — all derived fields auto-calculated
> order = PurchaseOrder(
>     vendor_name="TechSupplies Inc",
>     items=[
>         {"name": "USB Cable",  "qty": 10, "price": 4.99},
>         {"name": "HDMI Cable", "qty": 5,  "price": 12.99},
>         {"name": "Mouse Pad",  "qty": 20, "price": 3.49},
>     ]
> )
>
> print(f"Order ID    : {order.order_id}")
> print(f"Vendor      : {order.vendor_name}")
> print(f"Items       : {order.item_count}")
> print(f"Subtotal    : ${order.subtotal:.2f}")
> print(f"Tax (8%)    : ${order.tax_amount:.2f}")
> print(f"Total       : ${order.total:.2f}")
> print(f"Integrity   : {order.verify_integrity()}")
> ```

sections.title: Dataclass Parameters — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What does `frozen=True` do and what are its trade-offs?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `frozen=True` makes instances immutable — any attempt to assign to a field raises `FrozenInstanceError`. It also enables `__hash__` generation (since immutable objects can safely be hashed). Benefits: (1) Hashable — can use as dict keys and set elements. (2) Thread-safe — immutable objects are inherently safe to share across threads. (3) Semantic clarity — signals "this is a value object, not mutable entity". (4) Cache-friendly — safe for use as `@functools.lru_cache` keys. Trade-offs: (1) Cannot modify in place — use `dataclasses.replace()` to create modified copies. (2) Slightly more overhead from the protection mechanism. (3) Cannot use mutable default values even more strictly. I use `frozen=True` for: value objects (Money, Color, Point, Version), configuration, events in event sourcing, cache keys.

**Q2. When would you use `order=True` and what does it generate?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `order=True` generates `__lt__`, `__le__`, `__gt__`, `__ge__` — making instances sortable and comparable with `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. It compares fields **in order of definition** — first field is primary sort key, second is secondary, etc. Use it when: (1) Objects have natural ordering (Priority, Version, Score). (2) You need to sort collections. (3) You want to use `min()`, `max()`, `sorted()`, or `heapq`. Important constraints: (1) `eq=True` is required for `order=True` (default is fine). (2) Cannot use `order=True` if you define any comparison methods manually. (3) If you only want some fields to participate in ordering, use `field(compare=False)` on others. In practice: I use `order=True` for Priority levels, Semantic Versions, Score rankings.

**Q3. What is `slots=True` and when should you use it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `slots=True` (Python 3.10+) adds `__slots__` to the generated class, which replaces the per-instance `__dict__` with a fixed array of attribute slots. Benefits: (1) **Memory**: ~30-50% less memory per instance — no `__dict__` overhead. (2) **Speed**: attribute access 10-15% faster (direct index vs hash lookup). (3) **Safety**: prevents accidental attribute creation (`obj.typo = value` fails). Use when: creating millions of instances (data pipelines, game entities, ML features), memory-constrained environments, performance-critical code. Trade-offs: (1) Can't add arbitrary attributes. (2) Doesn't work with some metaclasses or multiple inheritance patterns. (3) Python 3.10+ only (use regular dataclass on older versions). In production data pipelines processing 100M+ records, `slots=True` can reduce memory by GBs.

**Q4. What happens to `__hash__` in different dataclass configurations?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Python's `__hash__` behavior in dataclasses follows careful rules: (1) `frozen=False, eq=True` (default): `__hash__` is set to `None` — class is unhashable. This is safe: mutable objects shouldn't be hashable (changing them would change their hash). (2) `frozen=True`: generates `__hash__` based on all fields — safe since immutable. (3) `eq=False`: inherits `__hash__` from parent (default `object.__hash__` = identity). (4) `unsafe_hash=True`: generates `__hash__` even for mutable class — dangerous! Only use when you're certain instances won't change while being used as hash keys. The default (mutable = unhashable) protects against the classic bug where you put an object in a set, modify it, and then can't find it anymore.

**Q5. What is the difference between `eq=False` and `order=False`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `eq=False` disables `__eq__` generation — equality comparison falls back to identity (`is`) comparison from `object`. Two instances are equal ONLY if they're the same object. `order=False` (default) disables ordering methods (`__lt__`, `__gt__`, etc.) — `<` and `>` comparisons raise `TypeError`. They're independent: `eq=True, order=False` (default) gives equality but no sorting. `eq=True, order=True` gives both. `eq=False, order=False` = reference comparison only. When would you use `eq=False`? When you have domain objects where equality is identity — like `Thread`, `Connection`, `Socket` objects where two connections are never "equal" even with same host/port.

sections.body:
**S1. You're implementing a priority queue for a task scheduler. How do you design the Task dataclass?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field
> from datetime import datetime
> import heapq
>
> @dataclass(order=True)
> class Task:
>     # Primary sort: priority (lower = higher priority, 1=critical)
>     priority:    int
>     # Secondary sort: deadline (earlier deadline = process first)
>     deadline:    str    # ISO format: "2024-01-15T10:00:00"
>     # Tertiary sort: creation order (FIFO for same priority+deadline)
>     sequence:    int    = field(default_factory=lambda: next(Task._counter))
>
>     # These fields don't affect ordering
>     task_id:     str    = field(default="", compare=False)
>     title:       str    = field(default="", compare=False)
>     assignee:    str    = field(default="", compare=False)
>     status:      str    = field(default="pending", compare=False, repr=False)
>
>     _counter = iter(range(10**9))  # class-level counter
>
>     def __post_init__(self):
>         if not self.task_id:
>             import uuid
>             self.task_id = str(uuid.uuid4())[:8]
>
>     def is_overdue(self) -> bool:
>         return datetime.fromisoformat(self.deadline) < datetime.now()
>
> # Priority queue using heapq
> class TaskScheduler:
>     def __init__(self):
>         self._queue = []
>
>     def add_task(self, task: Task):
>         heapq.heappush(self._queue, task)  # needs order=True!
>         print(f"  Added: [{task.priority}] {task.title}")
>
>     def get_next(self) -> Task:
>         return heapq.heappop(self._queue)
>
>     def peek_next(self) -> Task:
>         return self._queue[0] if self._queue else None
>
>     def pending_count(self) -> int:
>         return len(self._queue)
>
> scheduler = TaskScheduler()
> scheduler.add_task(Task(3,"2024-12-31T23:59:00",title="Write docs",assignee="Alice"))
> scheduler.add_task(Task(1,"2024-01-15T09:00:00",title="Fix prod bug!",assignee="Bob"))
> scheduler.add_task(Task(2,"2024-01-16T12:00:00",title="Deploy feature",assignee="Alice"))
> scheduler.add_task(Task(1,"2024-01-14T08:00:00",title="DB down URGENT",assignee="Charlie"))
>
> print(f"\nProcessing {scheduler.pending_count()} tasks in priority order:")
> while scheduler.pending_count() > 0:
>     task = scheduler.get_next()
>     print(f"  [{task.priority}] {task.title:<25} → {task.assignee}")
> ```

**S2. You're building a caching system where cache keys must be hashable and immutable. How do you use frozen dataclasses?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field
> from functools import lru_cache
> from typing import Tuple, Optional
>
> @dataclass(frozen=True)
> class QueryKey:
>     """Immutable, hashable cache key for database queries"""
>     table:   str
>     filters: Tuple[Tuple[str, str, object], ...] = ()  # ((col, op, val), ...)
>     order_by:Tuple[str, ...] = ()
>     limit:   Optional[int]   = None
>     offset:  int = 0
>
>     @classmethod
>     def build(cls, table: str, filters=None, order_by=None,
>               limit=None, offset=0) -> "QueryKey":
>         return cls(
>             table   = table,
>             filters = tuple(tuple(f) for f in (filters or [])),
>             order_by= tuple(order_by or []),
>             limit   = limit,
>             offset  = offset,
>         )
>
>     def to_sql(self) -> str:
>         sql = f"SELECT * FROM {self.table}"
>         if self.filters:
>             conditions = " AND ".join(f"{c} {op} ?" for c, op, _ in self.filters)
>             sql += f" WHERE {conditions}"
>         if self.order_by:
>             sql += f" ORDER BY {', '.join(self.order_by)}"
>         if self.limit:
>             sql += f" LIMIT {self.limit}"
>         if self.offset:
>             sql += f" OFFSET {self.offset}"
>         return sql
>
> class QueryCache:
>     """Cache using frozen dataclass as key"""
>     def __init__(self, max_size=100):
>         self._cache = {}
>         self._max   = max_size
>
>     def get(self, key: QueryKey):
>         result = self._cache.get(key)  # hash-based lookup — O(1)!
>         if result:
>             print(f"  🎯 Cache HIT: {key.table}")
>         return result
>
>     def set(self, key: QueryKey, value):
>         self._cache[key] = value
>         print(f"  💾 Cache SET: {key.table}")
>
> cache = QueryCache()
>
> # Same logical query = same key = cache hit
> q1 = QueryKey.build("users", [("active","=",True)], ["name"], limit=10)
> q2 = QueryKey.build("users", [("active","=",True)], ["name"], limit=10)
>
> print(f"q1 == q2: {q1 == q2}")   # True
> print(f"q1 is q2: {q1 is q2}")   # False (different objects)
> print(f"Same hash: {hash(q1) == hash(q2)}")  # True
>
> # Works as dict key because it's frozen/hashable
> cache.set(q1, [{"id":1,"name":"Alice"}, {"id":2,"name":"Bob"}])
> result = cache.get(q2)  # cache HIT even though different object!
> print(f"Result: {result}")
>
> print(f"\nSQL: {q1.to_sql()}")
>
> # Also works with lru_cache!
> @lru_cache(maxsize=256)
> def expensive_query(key: QueryKey):
>     print(f"  🔍 Executing: {key.to_sql()}")
>     return [{"fake": "data"}]
>
> expensive_query(q1)  # executes
> expensive_query(q2)  # cache hit (same frozen key!)
> print(f"Cache info: {expensive_query.cache_info()}")
> ```

**S3. You need a high-performance event processing system creating millions of event objects. How do you optimize the dataclass?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field
> import time, sys, tracemalloc
>
> # ❌ Regular dataclass — slower, more memory
> @dataclass
> class EventRegular:
>     event_id:  str
>     event_type:str
>     timestamp: float
>     user_id:   str
>     payload:   dict = field(default_factory=dict)
>
> # ✅ Optimized with slots=True + frozen=True
> @dataclass(slots=True, frozen=True)
> class EventOptimized:
>     event_id:  str
>     event_type:str
>     timestamp: float
>     user_id:   str
>     # Note: can't use mutable default with frozen
>     # Use tuple instead of dict for immutable payload
>
> # Performance comparison
> N = 100_000
>
> # Memory test - Regular
> tracemalloc.start()
> events_r = [
>     EventRegular(f"E{i}", "click", time.time(), f"U{i%1000}")
>     for i in range(N)
> ]
> mem_r = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[1]
> tracemalloc.stop()
>
> # Memory test - Optimized
> tracemalloc.start()
> events_o = [
>     EventOptimized(f"E{i}", "click", time.time(), f"U{i%1000}")
>     for i in range(N)
> ]
> mem_o = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[1]
> tracemalloc.stop()
>
> print(f"{'='*50}")
> print(f"Creating {N:,} events:")
> print(f"  Regular  memory: {mem_r/1024/1024:.1f} MB")
> print(f"  Optimized memory: {mem_o/1024/1024:.1f} MB")
> print(f"  Savings: {(1 - mem_o/mem_r)*100:.0f}%")
>
> # Object size
> print(f"\nSingle object size:")
> print(f"  Regular  : {sys.getsizeof(events_r[0])} bytes")
> print(f"  Optimized: {sys.getsizeof(events_o[0])} bytes")
>
> # Optimized = hashable = can use set for dedup
> unique_events = set(events_o[:100])  # Works because frozen!
> print(f"\nDeduplicated: {len(unique_events)} unique events")
> ```

sections.title: Special Methods: __post_init__, InitVar, ClassVar — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. When is `__post_init__` called and what can you do in it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `__post_init__` is called by the dataclass-generated `__init__` as its LAST action, after all field assignments are complete. You can: validate field values and raise exceptions, compute derived fields (especially `init=False` fields), transform/normalize input values (lowercase email, strip whitespace), set up relationships between fields, register the instance in a class-level registry. Important: if you define a field with `init=False`, its default/default_factory runs first, then `__post_init__` can override it. If you have `InitVar` fields, they're passed as additional parameters to `__post_init__`. I use `__post_init__` as a comprehensive validation and initialization hook in all my domain model classes.

**Q2. What is `InitVar` and how does it differ from a regular field?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `InitVar[T]` marks a parameter that's included in `__init__` but is NOT stored as an instance attribute. It's passed to `__post_init__` as a parameter and then disappears — it's a "use once" initialization input. Differences from regular field: (1) NOT stored — `hasattr(instance, 'field_name')` is False after init. (2) NOT in `__repr__` — never shown. (3) NOT in `__eq__` — doesn't affect equality. (4) NOT in `asdict()` or `astuple()`. Common uses: passwords (hash them, don't store them), connection strings (extract components, discard), configuration objects (compute derived config, don't store raw input), any "catalyst" input that triggers computation but isn't itself the result.

**Q3. What is `ClassVar` and why is it needed in dataclasses?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `ClassVar[T]` (from `typing`) marks a class-level variable that should NOT be treated as a dataclass field. Without `ClassVar`, any annotated class attribute becomes a field — included in `__init__`, `__repr__`, and `__eq__`. With `ClassVar`: completely invisible to the dataclass machinery. Use `ClassVar` for: (1) Class-level registries: `_instances: ClassVar[dict] = {}`. (2) Constants: `MAX_SIZE: ClassVar[int] = 100`. (3) Counters: `_id_counter: ClassVar[int] = 0`. (4) Cached class-level data: `_valid_values: ClassVar[set] = {"a", "b"}`. Without `ClassVar`, Python would try to include these in `__init__` which usually causes errors or confusing behavior.

**Q4. Can you call `super().__post_init__()` in inherited dataclasses?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Yes, and it's important for inherited dataclasses with `__post_init__`. When you have a parent dataclass with `__post_init__` and a child that also has `__post_init__`, you should call `super().__post_init__()` in the child to ensure parent validation/setup runs:
>
> ```python
> @dataclass
> class Base:
>     name: str
>     def __post_init__(self):
>         if not self.name:
>             raise ValueError("Name required")
>         self.name = self.name.strip()
>
> @dataclass
> class Child(Base):
>     age: int
>     def __post_init__(self):
>         super().__post_init__()  # Run parent validation first!
>         if self.age < 0:
>             raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative")
> ```
>
> If you forget `super().__post_init__()`, parent validation is skipped silently — a hard-to-find bug. With `InitVar` in parent, things get more complex — parent's `__post_init__` signature must match.

**Q5. How do you handle `InitVar` in inherited dataclasses?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `InitVar` in inherited dataclasses requires careful handling because `__post_init__` signature changes:
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, InitVar
>
> @dataclass
> class BaseUser:
>     username: str
>     plain_password: InitVar[str]  # passed to __post_init__
>
>     def __post_init__(self, plain_password: str):
>         self.password_hash = hash(plain_password)
>
> @dataclass
> class AdminUser(BaseUser):
>     role: str = "admin"
>     admin_code: InitVar[str] = ""  # additional InitVar in child
>
>     def __post_init__(self, plain_password: str, admin_code: str):
>         # Must accept ALL InitVars — both parent and child
>         super().__post_init__(plain_password)  # pass parent's InitVar
>         if admin_code != "ADMIN-SECRET":
>             raise ValueError("Invalid admin code")
> ```
>
> The child's `__post_init__` must accept all `InitVar` parameters from the entire hierarchy (parent first, then child). This ordering matches the generated `__init__` parameter order.

sections.body:
**S1. Build a domain model for a hospital patient system using all the special methods.**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field, InitVar
> from typing import ClassVar, List, Dict, Optional
> from datetime import datetime, date
> import uuid, re
>
> @dataclass
> class Patient:
>     # ClassVar: hospital-wide patient registry
>     _registry:     ClassVar[Dict[str, "Patient"]] = {}
>     _total_count:  ClassVar[int]                  = 0
>     MRN_PREFIX:    ClassVar[str]                  = "MRN"
>
>     # Regular fields (user provides)
>     first_name:    str
>     last_name:     str
>     date_of_birth: str    # "YYYY-MM-DD"
>     gender:        str
>
>     # InitVar: SSN for identity verification (compute ID, don't store SSN)
>     ssn:           InitVar[str]
>
>     # Optional fields
>     blood_type:    Optional[str]  = None
>     allergies:     List[str]      = field(default_factory=list)
>     phone:         str            = ""
>
>     # Auto-generated (init=False)
>     patient_id:    str            = field(default="", init=False)
>     mrn:           str            = field(default="", init=False)
>     age:           int            = field(default=0, init=False)
>     full_name:     str            = field(default="", init=False)
>     registered_at: str            = field(default="", init=False)
>     visits:        List[dict]     = field(default_factory=list, init=False)
>
>     # Sensitive — hash of SSN for dedup (never store SSN)
>     _ssn_hash:     str            = field(default="", init=False, repr=False)
>
>     VALID_GENDERS   = {"M", "F", "X", "Other"}
>     VALID_BLOOD_TYPES= {"A+","A-","B+","B-","AB+","AB-","O+","O-", None}
>
>     def __post_init__(self, ssn: str):
>         errors = []
>
>         # Validate gender
>         if self.gender not in self.VALID_GENDERS:
>             errors.append(f"Invalid gender: {self.gender}. Valid: {self.VALID_GENDERS}")
>
>         # Validate blood type
>         if self.blood_type not in self.VALID_BLOOD_TYPES:
>             errors.append(f"Invalid blood type: {self.blood_type}")
>
>         # Validate date of birth
>         try:
>             dob = date.fromisoformat(self.date_of_birth)
>             today = date.today()
>             self.age = (today - dob).days // 365
>             if self.age < 0 or self.age > 150:
>                 errors.append(f"Invalid date of birth: {self.date_of_birth}")
>         except ValueError:
>             errors.append(f"Invalid date format (use YYYY-MM-DD): {self.date_of_birth}")
>
>         # Validate SSN format (simplified)
>         ssn_clean = re.sub(r'[-\s]', '', ssn)
>         if not re.match(r'^\d{9}$', ssn_clean):
>             errors.append("Invalid SSN format")
>
>         if errors:
>             raise ValueError("Patient registration failed:\n" +
>                            "\n".join(f"  - {e}" for e in errors))
>
>         # Compute fields
>         self.full_name     = f"{self.first_name.strip()} {self.last_name.strip()}"
>         self.patient_id    = str(uuid.uuid4())[:8].upper()
>         Patient._total_count += 1
>         self.mrn           = f"{self.MRN_PREFIX}-{Patient._total_count:06d}"
>         self.registered_at = datetime.now().isoformat()
>
>         # Store SSN hash for deduplication — never store SSN itself
>         import hashlib
>         self._ssn_hash = hashlib.sha256(ssn_clean.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
>
>         # Register
>         Patient._registry[self.patient_id] = self
>
>     def add_visit(self, reason: str, doctor: str):
>         self.visits.append({
>             "visit_id": str(uuid.uuid4())[:8],
>             "date":     datetime.now().isoformat(),
>             "reason":   reason,
>             "doctor":   doctor,
>         })
>
>     @classmethod
>     def total_patients(cls) -> int:
>         return cls._total_count
>
> # Demo
> p1 = Patient("Alice","Johnson","1990-05-15","F","123-45-6789",
>              blood_type="A+", allergies=["Penicillin","Aspirin"])
> p2 = Patient("Bob","Smith","1985-08-22","M","987-65-4321",
>              blood_type="O-")
>
> p1.add_visit("Annual checkup", "Dr. Smith")
> p1.add_visit("Follow-up", "Dr. Jones")
>
> print(f"Patient : {p1.full_name}")
> print(f"MRN     : {p1.mrn}")
> print(f"Age     : {p1.age}")
> print(f"Visits  : {len(p1.visits)}")
> print(f"Total   : {Patient.total_patients()} patients registered")
> print(f"\nRepr (SSN not shown): {p1}")
> ```

**S2 & S3** — Similar detailed patterns applying InitVar for secrets, ClassVar for registries, and `__post_init__` for complex validation in e-commerce and authentication systems.

sections.title: Inheritance in Dataclasses — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What are the field ordering rules in inherited dataclasses?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> In inherited dataclasses, the generated `__init__` puts parent fields FIRST, then child fields, in definition order. The critical constraint: Python function signature rules apply — you can't have a required parameter (no default) after an optional parameter (has default). So if a parent has any field with a default, ALL child fields must also have defaults. Solutions: (1) `KW_ONLY` sentinel — marks all following fields as keyword-only, bypassing the ordering constraint. (2) Give all child fields defaults. (3) Use composition instead of inheritance when the hierarchy becomes too complex. (4) `dataclass(kw_only=True)` on child — all child fields become keyword-only. I've seen many bugs from this constraint — it's one of the first things I check in dataclass code reviews.

**Q2. How does `__eq__` work in inherited dataclasses?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> The child dataclass generates its own `__eq__` that compares ALL fields — both parent fields and child fields. Two objects are equal only if they're the same type AND all fields match:
>
> ```python
> @dataclass
> class Animal:
>     name: str
>
> @dataclass
> class Dog(Animal):
>     breed: str
>
> a = Animal("Rex")
> d = Dog("Rex", "Labrador")
> print(a == d)   # False — different types!
> print(d == Dog("Rex", "Labrador"))  # True
> ```
>
> Important: `@dataclass(eq=False)` on either parent or child affects which `__eq__` is used. If child doesn't generate `__eq__` (eq=False), it inherits parent's — which only compares parent fields. This can cause subtle bugs where two different Dogs with same name but different breeds compare as equal.

**Q3. Can you use abstract base classes with dataclasses?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Yes! Combine `@dataclass` with `ABC`:
>
> ```python
> from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
> from dataclasses import dataclass
>
> @dataclass
> class Shape(ABC):
>     color: str = "black"
>
>     @abstractmethod
>     def area(self) -> float:
>         ...
>
>     @abstractmethod
>     def perimeter(self) -> float:
>         ...
>
> @dataclass
> class Circle(Shape):
>     radius: float = 1.0
>
>     def area(self) -> float:
>         import math
>         return math.pi * self.radius ** 2
>
>     def perimeter(self) -> float:
>         import math
>         return 2 * math.pi * self.radius
>
> # Can't instantiate abstract class:
> # Shape("red")  → TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class
> c = Circle("red", 5.0)  # Works!
> ```
>
> The decorator order matters: `@dataclass` should come BEFORE `(ABC)` in the class definition, though usually just inheriting from an abstract dataclass parent works fine. I use this pattern for domain model hierarchies where all entities share common behavior but differ in specific implementations.

**Q4. How do you override a parent field in a child dataclass?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Simply re-declare the field in the child with the same name. The child's declaration completely replaces the parent's:
>
> ```python
> @dataclass
> class Vehicle:
>     fuel_type: str = "Gasoline"
>     max_speed_kmh: int = 200
>
> @dataclass
> class ElectricCar(Vehicle):
>     # Override parent's default
>     fuel_type: str = "Electric"  # replaces parent's "Gasoline"
>     # Override with new constraints (via field())
>     max_speed_kmh: int = field(default=250, compare=False)
>
>     battery_kwh: float = 75.0  # new field
> ```
>
> The child's `__init__` will use the child's version of the field. Important caveat: if you override with `field()`, you lose the parent's field metadata. If parent had `compare=False`, child's re-declaration starts fresh. I document field overrides clearly in code comments because they can be surprising to maintainers.

**Q5. What happens with `__post_init__` in an inheritance chain?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `__post_init__` is NOT automatically chained — if both parent and child define it, only the child's runs (standard Python method resolution). To run parent's `__post_init__`: explicitly call `super().__post_init__()` in child. With `InitVar`: child's `__post_init__` must accept ALL `InitVar` parameters from the entire hierarchy — both parent's and child's — in order (parent first). Pattern I always follow:
>
> ```python
> @dataclass
> class Base:
>     name: str
>     setup_code: InitVar[str]
>     def __post_init__(self, setup_code: str):
>         self.name = self.name.upper()
>         # process setup_code
>
> @dataclass
> class Child(Base):
>     extra: str = ""
>     child_code: InitVar[str] = ""
>     def __post_init__(self, setup_code: str, child_code: str):
>         super().__post_init__(setup_code)  # MUST pass InitVar args!
>         self.extra = child_code.upper()
> ```
>
> Forgetting `super().__post_init__()` is a common bug — parent validation silently skipped.

SMS has character limit > _MAX_LENGTH: int = field(default=160, init=False, repr=False) > > def __post_init__(self): > super().__post_init__() > import re > clean = re.sub(r'\D', '', self.phone_number) > if len(clean) < 10: > raise ValueError(f"Invalid phone: {self.phone_number}") > if len(self.body) > self._MAX_LENGTH: > self.body = self.body[:157] + "..." # truncate > > def send(self) -> bool: > print(f"📱 SMS → {self.phone_number}: {self.body[:30]}...") > self.mark_sent() > return True > > # Push notification > @dataclass > class PushNotification(Notification): > device_token: str = "" > platform: str = "ios" # ios, android, web > badge_count: int = 0 > sound: str = "default" > deep_link: str = "" > action_data: Dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict) > > def __post_init__(self): > super().__post_init__() > if self.platform not in {"ios", "android", "web"}: > raise ValueError(f"Invalid platform: {self.platform}") > > def send(self) -> bool: > print(f"🔔 Push [{self.platform}] → {self.device_token[:8]}...: {self.title}") > self.mark_sent() > return True > > # Notification dispatcher > class NotificationService: > def __init__(self): > self.sent_count = 0 > self.failed_count= 0 > > def dispatch(self, notification: Notification) -> bool: > try: > success = notification.send() > if success: > self.sent_count += 1 > return success > except Exception as e: > notification.mark_failed(str(e)) > self.failed_count += 1 > return False > > def dispatch_all(self, notifications: List[Notification]) -> Dict[str, int]: > for n in notifications: > self.dispatch(n) > return {"sent": self.sent_count, "failed": self.failed_count} > > # Demo > service = NotificationService() > > notifications = [ > EmailNotification( > recipient_id="U001", title="Welcome!", body="Thanks for joining", > priority="high", to_email="alice@example.com", > cc=["manager@company.com"] > ), > SMSNotification( > recipient_id="U001", title="OTP", body="Your OTP is 123456", > priority="critical", phone_number="+1-800-555-1234" > ), > PushNotification( > recipient_id="U001", title="New message", body="Bob sent you a message", > priority="normal", device_token="abc123def456", > platform="ios", deep_link="/messages/123" > ), > ] > > results = service.dispatch_all(notifications) > print(f"\nResults: {results}") > > # All are Notification instances > for n in notifications: > print(f" {type(n).__name__:<20}: status={n.status}, id={n.notification_id}") > ``` **S2 & S3** — Similar detailed patterns for payment processing hierarchy (Payment → CreditCardPayment, BankTransfer, CryptoPayment) and employee hierarchy (Employee → Manager, Developer, SalesRep).

sections.title: Advanced Dataclass Features — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is the difference between `asdict()` and manually converting to dict?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `asdict()` performs a **deep recursive conversion** — nested dataclasses are also converted to dicts, lists of dataclasses become lists of dicts, tuples become lists. Manual `obj.__dict__` gives a shallow dict of the instance's namespace — nested dataclasses remain as objects. `vars(obj)` is similar. `asdict()` advantages: (1) Works recursively — no manual handling of nested objects. (2) Copies data (not references) — safe to modify result without affecting original. (3) Handles all nested types consistently. (4) Works correctly with `field(repr=False)` — still included in asdict (asdict includes ALL fields). Caveat: `asdict()` doesn't include properties — only actual fields. For JSON serialization of complex types (datetime, Decimal), you still need a custom JSON encoder.

**Q2. How does `replace()` work and what are its use cases?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `replace(instance, **changes)` creates a NEW instance of the same class with specified fields changed, all other fields copied from the original. It calls `__init__` with the new values — so `__post_init__` runs again on the copy. Critical for `frozen=True` dataclasses where you can't modify in place. Use cases: (1) Immutable state management (Redux-like patterns). (2) Creating test fixtures with slight variations. (3) Functional update patterns. (4) Configuration variants (prod → dev). (5) Updating domain objects without mutation. Important: `replace()` doesn't work with `init=False` fields — you can't pass them as arguments. Post-init computed fields are recalculated. In event sourcing, I use `replace()` to apply events to immutable state objects.

**Q3. What does `fields()` return and how do you use it for metaprogramming?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `fields(class_or_instance)` returns a tuple of `Field` objects — one for each field. Each `Field` has: `name`, `type`, `default`, `default_factory`, `repr`, `compare`, `hash`, `init`, `metadata`. Use cases: (1) **Dynamic validation** — iterate fields, check constraints from metadata. (2) **Serialization** — know which fields to serialize and how. (3) **Documentation generation** — read field metadata to generate API docs. (4) **Form generation** — create form widgets from field definitions. (5) **ORM integration** — map fields to database columns. (6) **Test data generation** — create random valid instances by inspecting types. I use `fields()` extensively in my generic serialization and validation libraries — it's what makes truly generic code possible.

**Q4. What is `make_dataclass()` and when would you use it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `make_dataclass(name, fields, ...)` creates a new dataclass class at runtime — dynamically, without writing class code. It's the programmatic equivalent of the `@dataclass` decorator. Use cases: (1) **Plugin systems** — load model definitions from config files. (2) **Code generation tools** — generate dataclasses from API schemas or database schemas. (3) **Test frameworks** — create test fixtures with arbitrary schemas. (4) **Dynamic forms** — build form models from database-stored field definitions. (5) **Schema-driven development** — OpenAPI spec → Python models. Alternatives: Pydantic's dynamic model creation is often better for validation-heavy use cases. `make_dataclass()` is a powerful escape hatch when you truly need runtime class generation.

**Q5. What is `is_dataclass()` and when is it useful?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `is_dataclass(obj)` returns `True` if `obj` is a dataclass class OR an instance of a dataclass. Use it for: (1) **Type guards in generic code** — before calling `asdict()`, `fields()`, etc. (2) **Serialization routers** — check if object is dataclass before using dataclass serialization. (3) **Validation frameworks** — handle dataclasses differently from plain dicts. (4) **Plugin registration** — verify plugins implement the expected dataclass interface.
>
> ```python
> def serialize(obj):
>     if dataclasses.is_dataclass(obj) and not isinstance(obj, type):
>         return asdict(obj)
>     elif hasattr(obj, '__dict__'):
>         return vars(obj)
>     else:
>         return str(obj)
> ```
>
> Note: `is_dataclass(MyClass)` is True for the class itself. `is_dataclass(instance)` is True for instances. To check instance specifically: `is_dataclass(obj) and not isinstance(obj, type)`.

quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: A dataclass is a Python decorator (@dataclass) introduced in Python 3.7 (PEP 557) that automatically generates boilerplate special methods for classes whose primary purpose is storing data. By default it generates: __init__() (constructor with all fields as parameters), __repr__() (human-readable string representation), and __eq__() (equality comparison that compares all fields).

Key differences: (1) Dataclasses require type annotations for all fields — they're not just code style, they're part of the dataclass specification.
